insight.title: Why Solving a Problem Makes it Look Bigger
insight.subtitle: Why your progress might look like a new setback

sections.text: When the British Army introduced steel helmets in WWI, hospital admissions for head injuries skyrocketed. Commanders were horrified, nearly banning the gear. In reality, soldiers who previously died were now surviving to be treated.
This is the "survivor’s bias" in reverse. We often measure failure by what we can see, forgetting that the most catastrophic failures are invisible because they leave no data behind to be counted.
In your work, improving a system often uncovers more errors. It looks like you are failing, but you are actually capturing data that used to be a silent, terminal disaster. Don't fear the numbers.
Try this today: When you face a new problem today, ask if it is actually a sign of hidden progress.
The absence of visible errors is often a sign of total failure, not perfect success.

news.title: Russian missiles and drones bombard Ukraine in hourslong attack
news.description: Russia hammered civilian areas of Ukraine with hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles in an attack that stretched for hours killing at least 16 people.
news.why: Supply chain hits mean you will wait longer for car repairs.

news.title: Foreign investors flee Thailand as Iran war, energy shock dash hope for economic revival
news.description: SINGAPORE - Foreign investors are selling Thai assets as an energy shock from the US-Israeli war on Iran threatens to snuff out hopes ​for an economic revival under Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and exposes the policy paralysis that is gripping Bangkok.
news.why: A weaker Thai currency makes your next vacation there much cheaper.

news.title: Oil Prices Steady as Traders Balance Diplomatic Progress With Physical Shortages
news.description: Oil prices were little changed as improving U.S.-Iran diplomacy competed with severe global supply tightness.
news.why: Tight supplies keep the cost of filling your car high.

news.title: Oil prices gain and Asian markets rise
news.description: Asian stocks are mostly higher and oil prices have steadied as investors watch closely prospects of a ceasefire extension in the Iran war and more talks between the U.S. and Iran.
news.why: Optimism over ceasefires helps protect the value of your stock investments.

news.title: Foreigners boost US Treasury holdings to record highs in February
news.description: Foreign holdings of Treasuries climbed to a ​record high in February, data showed on Wednesday, rising for a second month ‌in a sign of strong appetite for U.S. debt even as markets reassess the outlook for the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy.
news.why: High demand for debt helps reduce your monthly home loan payments.

news.title: Rising food prices and a weak monsoon pose risks: India must act early to protect the most vulnerable
news.description: Food inflation has been outpacing overall inflation since January. It’s headed higher. War-driven cost pressures could combine with El Niño dryness this year to spell misery for multitudes. The Centre has foodgrain buffer stocks—but should draw up other plans.
news.why: A weak monsoon will make your fresh produce more expensive.

news.title: Wheat inflation may be triggered by April’s extreme weather patterns
news.description: India could see a dip of at least 10-15% in wheat production in the country. The worst hit state is Punjab
news.why: Low wheat production may cause bread shortages at your local store.

news.title: Vietnam's To Lam meets Xi in four-day trip to China
news.description: CHINA’S President Xi Jinping called to prioritise infrastructure connectivity with Vietnam, alongside co-operation on emerging fields such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors, during a meeting Wednesday with Vietnam’s newly elected president.Vietnamese President To Lam’s four-day trip to China, which began on Tuesday, is his first overseas trip since he was elected last week, signalling his foreign policy priorities and stronger ties between the two Communist nations.
news.why: Better rail links will shorten delivery times for your online orders.

news.title: China's solar producers say overcapacity unlikely to be solved by war-induced renewables demand
news.description: As of 2025, China's solar factories had enough capacity to cover the estimated global demand this year nearly twice over, even after taking into account the Iran war impact in its demand forecast, Morningstar estimates
news.why: Oversupply means buying solar panels for your home will cost less.

news.title: Apple Pushes Siri Programmers to Adopt AI Coding Tools
news.description: Apple mandates AI coding bootcamp for Siri engineers as development tools reshape tech workflowsApple is requiring a significant portion of its Siri programming team to attend a wee...
news.why: Your phone assistant will soon handle complex voice commands more reliably.

news.title: New imaging tools help cancer researchers see inside living cells
news.description: A new study co-led by an Oregon Health & Science University researcher describes a breakthrough in microscopy tools that could dramatically expand how cancer biology labs study the inner workings of living cells. The research, published in Nature Methods, introduces a series of fluorescent dyes that make it much easier to take ultra‑detailed images of living cells. These tools allow scientists to watch important cancer‑related processes as they happen, instead of relying only on still images of fixed cells.
news.why: New cell imaging will speed up your access to life-saving treatments.

news.title: Scientists discover hidden ocean methane source that could worsen global warming
news.description: Scientists have discovered that methane in the open ocean is produced by microbes under nutrient-poor conditions, solving a long-standing mystery. As warming oceans reduce nutrient mixing, these methane-producing microbes may thrive. This could lead to increased methane emissions from the sea. The result is a potential feedback loop that could intensify climate change.
news.why: Rising climate risks will likely increase your home insurance premiums.
